citation.title: On Counterfactual Metrics for Social Welfare: Incentives, Ranking, and Information Asymmetry

standing_assumptions:
Setting: a principal-agent model of quality metrics. A principal rewards (or ranks) an agent through a reward function $w$ of the data it observes; the agent chooses a treatment rule $\pi$ to maximize its expected reward; welfare and regret are defined from potential outcomes. Expectations are over the i.i.d. draw of the treatment population, the treatment randomization and, where it is random, the estimator $\hat\mu_0$. The pages of the published PDF carry no page numbers; every location below is a one-based PDF page of main.pdf (28 pp.; pp. 13-28 are the Supplementary Materials). Transcribed from the page images.

(S1) PDF p. 3, Section 2, 'Formal model': 'We suppose that a single agent has access to independently and identically distributed samples of characteristics $X_i \in \mathcal X$ for $i \in \{1,...,n\}$ treatment units (referred to generally as the treatment population). The agent assigns a binary treatment according to treatment rule $\pi : \mathcal X \to [0,1]$, and we use $T_i^\pi \in \{0,1\}$ to denote a Bernoulli random variable indicating the realizations of the treatment rule: $\pi(X_i) = P(T_i^\pi = 1|X_i)$. This framework allows for $T^\pi$ to be either stochastic or deterministic.' 'Let $Y_i(t)$ be the potential outcome if the patient had received treatment $t \in \{0,1\}$. Let $Y_i \in \mathbb R$ denote the observed outcome under treatment assignments $Y_i = Y_i(T_i^\pi)$ under the Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA) (Rubin, 1980), which implies the consistency and non-interference assumptions. Let $\tau(X) = E[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)|X]$ denote the conditional average treatment effect given covariates $X$, and let $\mu_t(X) = E[Y_i(t)|X]$ denote the conditional mean of the potential outcome under treatment $t$.'

(S2) PDF p. 3, Section 2: 'We suppose that the principal observes $\{X_i, T_i^\pi\}_{i=1}^n$ (also denoted $\mathbf X, \mathbf T^\pi$) for all units, and $Y_i$ for all units for which $T_i^\pi = 1$ (denoted $\mathbf Y$). The principal must then choose a reward function $w : \mathcal X^n \times \{0,1\}^n \times \mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R$ with which to reward the agent.' 'Turning to our behavioral assumption, we consider an agent that is risk neutral and maximizes their expected reward. That is, the agent chooses the treatment rule $\pi$ from their set of possible treatment rules $\Pi$ that maximizes $E[w(\mathbf X, \mathbf T^\pi, \mathbf Y)]$. Let $\pi^w \in \arg\max_{\pi\in\Pi} E[w(\mathbf X, \mathbf T^\pi, \mathbf Y)]$ denote this best response. In maximizing this expected reward, we assume that the agent knows $\mu_t(x)$ for all $x \in \mathcal X$ and $t \in \{0,1\}$. Note that there is no explicit model of the agent's cost here to keep the focus on incentives induced by accountability metrics alone, and all budget constraints are contained in the agent's feasible set of treatment rules $\Pi$.' Appendix B.1 (PDF p. 14): 'Let $\pi^w$ denote the agent's best response for the reward function $w$: $\pi^w = \arg\max_{\pi\in\Pi} E[w(\mathbf X, \mathbf T^\pi, \mathbf Y)]$.'

(S3) PDF p. 3, Section 2, 'Total welfare and regret': 'for a given treatment rule $\pi$, we define the total effect of treatment on welfare as $V(\pi) = E[Y_i(T_i^\pi) - Y_i(0)]$.' 'we define the regret for a given policy $\pi$ compared to the best feasible policy in $\Pi$ to be $R(\pi) = \max_{\tilde\pi\in\Pi} V(\tilde\pi) - V(\pi)$.'

(S4) Reward functions. PDF p. 4: 'Reward Function 1 (ATO): $w_{\mathrm{ATO}}(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi,\mathbf Y)=\begin{cases}\frac{\sum_{i=1}^nY_iT_i^\pi}{\sum_{i=1}^nT_i^\pi}&\sum_{i=1}^nT_i^\pi>0,\\0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$' PDF p. 4: 'Reward Function 2 (ATT): $w_{\mathrm{ATT}}(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi,\mathbf Y)=\begin{cases}\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-\hat\mu_0(X_i))T_i^\pi}{\sum_{i=1}^nT_i^\pi}&\sum_{i=1}^nT_i^\pi>0,\\0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$' PDF p. 5: 'Reward Function 3 (TT): $w_{\mathrm{TT}}(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi,\mathbf Y)=\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-\hat\mu_0(X_i))T_i^\pi$.' PDF p. 6: 'Reward Function 4 (Weighted TT): $w^g_{\mathrm{TT}}(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi,\mathbf Y)=\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-\hat\mu_0(X_i))T_i^\pi g(X_i)$.' PDF p. 15 (Appendix B.2): 'Reward Function 5 (TO): $w_{\mathrm{TO}}(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi,\mathbf Y)=\sum_{i=1}^nY_iT_i^\pi$. (1)'

(S5) PDF p. 4, Section 3: 'Assumption 1. The principal accesses an estimator $\hat\mu_0(x)$ which is unbiased: $E[\hat\mu_0(x)] = \mu_0(x)\ \forall x \in \mathcal X$.' The paper's example (p. 4): 'suppose the principal has access to an auxiliary data source $\{X'_j, T'_j, Y'_j\}_{j=1}^m$, with outcomes for untreated patients with $T'_j = 0$, collected from clinical trials or observational data.' Appendix D.2 (PDF p. 21) writes $\hat\mu_0^{\mathcal Q}(x)$ for the estimate 'from auxiliary data $\{X'_j,T'_j,Y'_j\}_{j=1}^m$ drawn i.i.d. from auxiliary dataset $\mathcal Q$', with $E[\hat\mu_0^{\mathcal Q}(x)] = E[Y'_j(0)|X'_j = x] = E[Y_i(0)|X_i = x]$.

(S6) PDF p. 15, proof of Proposition 6: 'Since $T_i^\pi$ only depends on $X_i$ by construction, we have the strong ignorability property that $\{Y_i(0), Y_i(1)\} \perp\!\!\!\perp T_i^\pi | X_i$.' PDF pp. 15-16: 'Lemma 1 (Optimal Treatment Rule). If the agent's treatment rule $\pi$ depends only on $X_i$, then the treatment rule $\pi^*$ that maximizes $V(\pi)$ is $\pi^*(x) = \begin{cases}1&\text{if }\tau(x)>0\\0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$' Its proof shows $V(\pi) = E[\tau(X_i)|T_i^\pi=1]P(T_i^\pi=1) = \int\tau(X_i)\pi(X_i)dP_{X_i}$. PDF p. 14, Appendix B.1: $\int f(Z)dP_Z$ denotes 'integration of the function $f(Z)$ with respect to the probability measure for the random variable $Z$'; 'the bold variable $\mathbf Z$' denotes 'the vector of i.i.d. random variables $\{Z_i\}_{i=1}^n$'; $\mathbb 1(x\in S)=1$ if $x\in S$ and $0$ otherwise.

(S7) Several agents. PDF p. 5, Section 4: 'Suppose each agent $k \in \{1,...,K\}$ observes its own sample of $n_k$ patients with covariates drawn i.i.d. from distribution $P_{X^k}$ with the same support $\mathcal X$. Each agent has different treatment effects, denoted by $\mu^k_t(x)$ and $\tau^k(x)$. For rankings to be meaningful, we assume that the untreated potential outcome is the same for all $k$: $\mu^k_0(x) = \mu_0(x)$ for all $k$.' 'the principal publishes score functions $\{w_k\}_{k=1}^K$, and each agent $k$ best responds individually with their own treatment policy $\pi_k$. The agents are then ranked from highest to lowest score function values.' Appendix C.1 (PDF p. 18) writes $\mathbf X^{(k)} = \{X_i^{(k)}\}_{i=1}^{n_k}$, $\mu_t^{(k)}(x) = E[Y_i^{(k)}(t)|X_i^{(k)} = x]$, $\tau^{(k)}(x) = E[Y_i^{(k)}(1) - Y_i^{(k)}(0)|X_i^{(k)} = x]$, $\mathbf T^{\pi_k} = \{T_i^{\pi_k}\}_{i=1}^{n_k}$, $Y_i^{(k)} = Y_i^{(k)}(T_i^{\pi_k})$, $\mathbf Y^{(k)} = \{Y_i^{(k)}\}_{i=1}^{n_k}$, and: 'the principal publishes score functions $w_k : \mathcal X^{n_k} \times \{0,1\}^{n_k} \times \mathbb R^{n_k} \to \mathbb R$, and each agent $k$ gets score $w_k(\mathbf X^{(k)}, \mathbf T^{\pi_k}, \mathbf Y^{(k)})$ after choosing their treatment policy $\pi_k$.' 'We assume that each agent seeks to maximize their individual ranking, and make the simplifying assumption that the agents act independently'. $X_0$ denotes a draw from the reference covariate population $P_{X_0}$ (p. 5).

(S8) Information asymmetry. PDF p. 6, Section 5: 'Suppose the agent observes additional covariates $U_i \in \mathcal U$, and selects a treatment rule $\pi : \mathcal X, \mathcal U \to [0,1]$. Suppose the principal still observes only $\{X_i, T_i^\pi, Y_i\}_{i=1}^n$, and chooses a reward function $w(\mathbf X, \mathbf T^\pi, \mathbf Y)$ that does not depend on $U_i$. Let $\mu_t(X,U) = E[Y_i(t)|X,U]$ and $\tau(X,U) = E[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)|X,U]$. The utility and regret are still defined as in Section 2.' 'Assumption 2 (Bounded Heteogeneity). The effect of $U_i$ on the conditional untreated potential outcome is bounded as $E[|\mu_0(X_i) - \mu_0(X_i,U_i)|] \leq \gamma_{\mathrm{marg}}$.' 'Note that $\mu_0(X_i) = E[\mu_0(X_i,U_i)|X_i]$.' Appendix D.1 (PDF p. 20): '$\pi(X,U) = P(T^\pi = 1|X,U)$' and 'The utility is still defined as in Section 2, and with the additional $U$ variable can be rewritten as $V(\pi) = E[\pi(X_i,U_i)\tau(X_i,U_i)]$.' The proof of Lemma 2 (PDF p. 21) uses 'ignorability in $X_i$ and $U_i$'.

(S9) Readings used throughout; they are implicit in the paper and not printed in these words. The units $(X_i, Y_i(0), Y_i(1))$ (with $U_i$ in the setting of (S8)) are i.i.d.; given the covariates the treatment indicators $T_i^\pi$ are independent across units, with $P(T_i^\pi=1|X_i)=\pi(X_i)$ (in (S8): $P(T_i^\pi=1|X_i,U_i)=\pi(X_i,U_i)$), and independent of the potential outcomes given $X_i$ (in (S8): given $(X_i,U_i)$); potential outcomes have finite means; a treatment rule is a fixed measurable function chosen before the data and the estimator are realized, and the agent's objective is the unconditional expected reward; '$\pi$ is unconstrained' and '$\Pi_k$ is unconstrained' mean that the feasible set is the set of all functions into $[0,1]$ (the appendix restatements say '$\Pi$ is the set of all functions $\pi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$'); where no such condition is stated, $\Pi$ is an arbitrary feasible set; $\pi^w$ is any element of the arg max in (S2), and a statement about the regret $R(\pi^w)$ is read for the best response the paper exhibits unless the target says otherwise; $g:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^+$ is read as a strictly positive weight (the proof of Theorem 1 uses 'Since $g(X_i)>0$').

What is and is not a target. Thirteen findings are confirmed errors whose correction changes a mathematical statement, a formula or a proof step, and each has a corrected-statement target: P006-E001 (Major), P006-E002 and P006-E009 (Moderate), and P006-E003, E005, E006, E007, E008, E013, E014, E015, N005 and N006 (Minor). Those for which the validator gave an exact counterexample (E001, E002, E003, E005, E006, E007, E008, N005) also have a counterexample target, and the three rated Moderate or above also have the statement as printed. P006-E009 is a reporting finding that is kept because it rests on an exact identity between two functionals of the same fitted effects, checkable from the numbers printed in Table 1, and the validator proved it in Lean. Not targets, because the correction changes no mathematical statement: P006-E010 (Moderate; the accuracy 0.6824 comes from a scoring line in the notebook), P006-E011 (Moderate; the released Stroke code credits any discharge alive where the printed score says within 14 days), P006-E012 and P006-N003 (code and data), P006-E018 (last printed digits), P006-N009 (the value 0.035 for a quantity computed from the Horse Colic data and the fitted model, not from anything printed), and P006-E016, P006-E017 and P006-N001 (citation, spelling and cross-reference misprints). P006-E004, N002, N007 and N010 were not confirmed, P006-N004 is a clarity note and P006-N008 is undetermined. Of the nine headline claims, P006-H1 to P006-H6 are mathematical and are covered as follows: H1 by P006-T29 (Proposition 1), P006-T1, T2, T26 (Proposition 6) and P006-T10, T11 (Theorem 4); H2 by P006-T3 (Proposition 2) and P006-T1, T2, T26 (Proposition 7); H3 by P006-T4, T6, T27 (Propositions 3 and 9; Lemma 1 is quoted in (S6)); H4 by P006-T14 (Definitions 1-2), P006-T30 (Proposition 4), P006-T7 (Theorem 1) and P006-T5, T12, T13 (Theorem 2); H5 by P006-T8 (Theorem 3, Lemma 2, Proposition 10) and P006-T25 (Proposition 5); H6 by P006-T15, T16, T17 (Theorem 5, Lemma 3). P006-H7, H8 and H9 are empirical results computed from two datasets (Tables 1-2, Figures 1-3) and are not targets.

canonical_claim.location: PDF p. 23 (Appendix D.3, first paragraph; Assumption 4; Theorem 5); PDF p. 24 (proof; Lemma 3)
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: PDF p. 23: 'Let $\hat\mu_0^\pi(X)=E[Y_i|T^\pi=0,X]$ denote the principal's estimate of the mean untreated potential outcome from the agent's data.' PDF p. 23: 'Assumption 4. The maximum effect of the unobserved attributes $U$ on the conditional untreated potential outcome is bounded on average. Define the maximum difference in the untreated potential outcome for a given $x,u$ to be $\Delta(x,u)=\max_{\tilde u\in\mathcal U}|\mu_0(x,u)-\mu_0(x,\tilde u)|$. The average difference is bounded as: $E[\Delta(X,U)]\leq\gamma_{\mathrm{max}}$.' Information asymmetry, $\mu_t(X,U)$, $\pi(X,U)=P(T^\pi=1|X,U)$, $V(\pi)=E[\pi(X_i,U_i)\tau(X_i,U_i)]$: PDF p. 6 and Appendix D.1, PDF p. 20, quoted in (S8). $w_{\mathrm{TT}}$: Reward Function 3, PDF p. 5, (S4). Lemma 2 (PDF p. 21), which gives the form of $S(\pi)$ when the estimate is a fixed function of $x$: quoted in target P006-T8. In the printed proof (PDF p. 24), $\Delta^\Pi(x,u)=\max_{\pi\in\Pi}|\hat\mu_0^\pi(x)-\mu_0(x,u)|$. Appendix A.1, item 2(b), PDF p. 13: 'Positivity: $P(T_i^\pi=0|X_i=x)>0$ for all $x\in\mathcal X$'. The maxima over $u$ and $\tilde u$ are as printed (attained, for instance for finite $\mathcal U$).
canonical_claim.note: From Sol's smallest_repair ('In D.3's symmetry sentence replace pi(x)>0 by pi(x)<1. In Theorem 5 and the appeal to Lemma 3 require, for every pi in Pi, P(T^pi=0|X=x)=E[1-pi(x,U)|X=x]>0 for P_X-almost every relevant x. The direct pointwise replacement pi(x,u)<1 is sufficient but stronger than necessary') and the validator's derivation, sections 3-4, equations (1)-(8). Here $\hat\mu_0^\pi$ is a population conditional mean, not a finite-sample estimate. The main text (PDF p. 7) refers to this result as 'a similar bound to Theorem 5', a cross-reference misprint for Theorem 3 (finding P006-N001, not a target).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proof of Proposition 1 (ATO Regret), second failure mode: the display $R(\pi^w)=(1-p)-p(\beta-1)=1-p\beta$
canonical_claim.location: PDF p. 17 (Appendix B.4, proof of Proposition 1)
canonical_claim.statement:
Printed statement refuted. PDF p. 17 (proof of Proposition 1): 'We construct an family of distributions for which the regret is unbounded. Let $\mathcal X=\{0,1\}$ with $P(X_i=1)=p$, and let $\mu_1(0)=0$, $\mu_1(1)=1$. Let $\mu_0(0)=\alpha$, and $\mu_0(1)=\beta$. Suppose $\Pi$ is the set of all functions $\pi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$. For $w_{\mathrm{ATO}}$, the agent's best response is $\pi^{w_{\mathrm{ATO}}}(0)=0$ and $\pi^{w_{\mathrm{ATO}}}(1)=1$.' PDF p. 17: 'A second failure mode would be if $\alpha=-1$, and $\beta>1$. Then the regret is given by $R(\pi^w)=(1-p)-p(\beta-1)=1-p\beta$. This is also unbounded for unbounded $\beta$.'

Counterexample (validator; exact): $p=\frac12$, $\alpha=-1$, $\beta=4$, $n=2$. Units are i.i.d. with $P(X_i=0)=P(X_i=1)=\frac12$ and deterministic potential outcomes given the covariate: $Y_i(0)=-1$, $Y_i(1)=0$ if $X_i=0$; $Y_i(0)=4$, $Y_i(1)=1$ if $X_i=1$. So $\mu_1=(0,1)$, $\mu_0=(-1,4)$, $\tau(0)=1$, $\tau(1)=-3$. $\Pi$ is the set of all functions $\pi:\{0,1\}\to[0,1]$, written $\pi=(a,b)$ with $a=\pi(0)$, $b=\pi(1)$.
(a) $\pi^w=(0,1)$ is the best response to $w_{\mathrm{ATO}}$ for the exact finite-sample reward: for every sample and every treatment vector $w_{\mathrm{ATO}}\leq\mathbb 1(X_1=1\text{ or }X_2=1)$, with equality under $\pi^w$, and $E[w_{\mathrm{ATO}}(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^{\pi^w},\mathbf Y)]=\frac34$; for a general $\pi=(a,b)$ the expected reward is $\frac{b(4-a-b)}{4}$, whose unique maximizer on $[0,1]^2$ is $(0,1)$.
(b) $V(a,b)=\frac12a-\frac32b$, so $\max_{\pi\in\Pi}V(\pi)=V(1,0)=\frac12$, $V(\pi^w)=-\frac32$ and $R(\pi^w)=\frac12-\left(-\frac32\right)=2$.
(c) The printed display gives $(1-p)-p(\beta-1)=1-p\beta=1-2=-1\neq2$; a regret is never negative.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $w_{\mathrm{ATO}}$: Reward Function 1, PDF p. 4, quoted in (S4). $V$, $R$, $\pi^w$: PDF p. 3, quoted in (S2)-(S3). The expected reward for general $\pi$ is the formula of target P006-T2 with $n=2$, $m=\mu_1$: $q=\frac{a+b}2$, $A=\frac b2$, $h_2(q)=2-q$.
canonical_claim.note: Validator's derivation, section 3; exact enumeration in runs/P006/validate/P006-E007/v1/artifact/check.py. Part (a) is included because the general rule of Proposition 6 is not valid (finding P006-E001), so the best response of the example is verified directly.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Appendix E.2.1 (Horse Colic dataset), the formula '$\mu_t(x)=\sigma(\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1^\top x+\hat\beta_2t+\hat\beta_3^\top xt)$' for the conditional mean of an outcome coded $1$ / $-1$
canonical_claim.statement:
Printed statement refuted. PDF p. 25, Appendix E.2.1: 'We removed all examples in which the horse was euthanized, and used the remaining "outcome" variable as $Y$, where we set $Y_i=1$ if the horse lived, and $Y_i=-1$ if the horse died.' 'To simulate $\mu_t(x)$, we assume that the outcome distribution takes the parametric form, $P(Y(t)=1|X=x)=\sigma(\beta_0+\beta_1^\top x+\beta_2t+\beta_3^\top xt)$ where $\sigma(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}$ is the standard logistic function. We trained a logistic regression model of $Y$ on $X$, $T$, and the interaction term $XT$ to estimate parameters $\hat\beta$, and used the resulting estimate to compute $\mu_t(x)=\sigma(\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1^\top x+\hat\beta_2t+\hat\beta_3^\top xt)$.' 'When computing agent best responses and regret, we take this function $\mu_t(x)$ to be given as synthetic mean conditional potential outcomes.'

Counterexample (validator; exact). $X=0$ with probability one, and the joint distribution of $(Y(0),Y(1))$ on $\{-1,1\}^2$ is: $(1,1)$ with probability $\frac18$, $(1,-1)$ with probability $\frac38$, $(-1,1)$ with probability $\frac18$, $(-1,-1)$ with probability $\frac38$.
(a) $P(Y(0)=1)=\frac12=\sigma(0)$ and $P(Y(1)=1)=\frac14=\sigma(-\log3)$, so the distribution belongs to the printed logistic model with $\beta_0=0$, $\beta_2=-\log3$, $\beta_1=\beta_3=0$.
(b) The conditional means of the outcome as coded are $\mu_0=E[Y(0)]=0$ and $\mu_1=E[Y(1)]=-\frac12$, and $\tau=-\frac12$.
(c) The printed formula gives $\mu_0=\sigma(0)=\frac12\neq0$ and $\mu_1=\sigma(-\log3)=\frac14\neq-\frac12$, and a difference of $-\frac14$.
(d) The rule $\pi^{w_{\mathrm{TO}}}(x)=\mathbb 1(\mu_1(x)>0)$ (PDF p. 15) treats nobody with the correct mean $\mu_1=-\frac12$ and everybody with the printed value $\frac14$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $\mu_t(X)=E[Y_i(t)|X]$ and $\tau$: PDF p. 3, quoted in (S1). Outcome coding (also PDF p. 7, Section 6): 'Our outcome of interest $Y$ is whether the horse lived ($Y=1$) or died ($Y=-1$).' $w_{\mathrm{TO}}$ and its unconstrained best response $\mathbb 1(\mu_1(x)>0)$: Appendix B.2, PDF p. 15, quoted in (S4).
canonical_claim.note: Validator's derivation, section 4; exact check in runs/P006/validate/P006-E008/v1/artifact/check.py. The released notebook already applies $2p-1$, so the published tables are on the correct scale; the error is in the printed formula.

We trained a logistic regression model of $Y$ on $X$, $T$, and the interaction term $XT$ to estimate parameters $\hat\beta$, and used the resulting estimate to compute $\mu_t(x)=\sigma(\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1^\top x+\hat\beta_2t+\hat\beta_3^\top xt)$.' 'When computing agent best responses and regret, we take this function $\mu_t(x)$ to be given as synthetic mean conditional potential outcomes.' $\mu_t(X)=E[Y_i(t)|X]$, $\tau(X)=E[Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)|X]$: PDF p. 3, quoted in (S1).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Appendix E.4 (Calculating $\gamma_{\mathrm{marg}}$), the empirical conditional mean $\mu_0(x)$, with the denominator $\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb 1(X_i=x)$ (printed as the single indicator $\mathbb 1(X_i=x)$)
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Assumption 2 and 'Note that $\mu_0(X_i)=E[\mu_0(X_i,U_i)|X_i]$': PDF p. 6, quoted in (S8). 'the full regression result' $\mu_0(x,u)$: the fitted synthetic means of Appendix E.2 (PDF p. 25).
canonical_claim.note: From Sol's smallest_repair in the batch verdict (denominator $\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb 1(X_i=x)$ with a positive count) and the section 'E015' of the batch derivations file, which gives the two-row example. Both released notebooks compute the group mean, so no reported value changes. A misprinted formula with a small formal content; (a)-(b) are the properties of the corrected definition that the paper uses.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Appendix A.1, item 2 ('Untreated patients in the treatment population'): conditions (a) and (b) as sufficient conditions for identifying $\mu_0(x)$ when outcomes are observed for a fraction of the untreated units
canonical_claim.statement:
Printed statement refuted. PDF p. 13, Appendix A.1, item 2: 'Untreated patients in the treatment population. In the main paper, we have assumed that the principal only observed outcomes $Y_i$ for treated units with $T_i^\pi=1$. If the principal also observed a fraction of outcomes for untreated units, with $T_i^\pi=0$, then these may also be incorporated into the estimate for $\hat\mu_0(x)$. Sufficient conditions for identifying $\mu_0(x)$ from a dataset of the agent's untreated units are: (a) No information asymmetry: the agent's treatment policy $\pi$ only depends on $X_i$. Under this assumption, we have no confounding: $\{Y_i(0),Y_i(1)\}\perp\!\!\!\perp T_i^\pi|X_i$. (b) Positivity: $P(T_i^\pi=0|X_i=x)>0$ for all $x\in\mathcal X$, and $Y_i$ is observed for a nonzero proportion of untreated units for all $x$.'

Counterexample (validator; exact). $\mathcal X=\{0\}$, $X=0$; $Y(1)=1$; $T\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\frac12)$ independent of $(Y(0),Y(1))$, so $\pi(0)=\frac12$ depends only on $X$; $R\in\{0,1\}$ indicates that the outcome $Y=Y(T)$ is observed, with $R=1$ whenever $T=1$. World A: $P(Y(0)=1)=P(Y(0)=0)=\frac12$, $P(R=1\mid Y(0)=0,T=0)=\frac14$, $P(R=1\mid Y(0)=1,T=0)=\frac34$. World B: $P(Y(0)=1)=\frac34$, $P(Y(0)=0)=\frac14$, $P(R=1\mid Y(0)=y,T=0)=\frac12$ for $y=0,1$. The observed record is $(X,T,R,Z)$ with $Z=Y$ if $R=1$ and $Z$ missing if $R=0$.
(a) Condition (a) holds in both worlds: $\{Y(0),Y(1)\}\perp\!\!\!\perp T\mid X$.
(b) Condition (b) holds in both worlds: $P(T=0\mid X=0)=\frac12>0$ and $P(R=1\mid T=0,X=0)=\frac12>0$.
(c) The distribution of the observed record is the same in both worlds: $(T,R,Z)=(0,0,\text{missing})$ with probability $\frac14$, $(0,1,0)$ with probability $\frac1{16}$, $(0,1,1)$ with probability $\frac3{16}$, $(1,1,1)$ with probability $\frac12$.
(d) $\mu_0(0)=\frac12$ in World A and $\mu_0(0)=\frac34$ in World B, so $\mu_0(0)$ is not a function of the distribution of the observed data.
(e) The mean of the observed untreated outcomes is $E[Y\mid X=0,T=0,R=1]=\frac34$ in both worlds; in World A it differs from $\mu_0(0)$ by $\frac14$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $\mu_0(x)=E[Y_i(0)|X_i=x]$, $Y_i=Y_i(T_i^\pi)$, $\pi(X_i)=P(T_i^\pi=1|X_i)$: PDF p. 3, quoted in (S1). The observation indicator $R$ is not a symbol of the paper; it formalizes 'observed a fraction of outcomes for untreated units'.
canonical_claim.note: Validator's derivation, section 3; exact check in runs/P006/validate/P006-N005/v1/artifact/check.py. A non-identification argument: two models that satisfy the listed conditions, give the same observed-data distribution and differ in the target. No theorem or experiment of the paper uses this data source.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proposition 6 (ATO Best Response) and Proposition 7 (ATT Best Response), as printed, with the same rules in Section 3
canonical_claim.location: PDF p. 15 (Proposition 6 and proof); PDF p. 16 (Proposition 7 and proof); PDF pp. 4-5 (Section 3)
canonical_claim.statement:
PDF p. 15: 'Proposition 6 (ATO Best Response). Suppose $\Pi$ is the set of all functions $\pi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, and suppose $X$ is a discrete random variable supported on $\mathcal X$. Then the agent's best response to $w_{\mathrm{ATO}}$ is: $\pi^{w_{\mathrm{ATO}}}(x)=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }x\in\arg\max_x\mu_1(x)\text{ and }\mu_1(x)>0\\0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$ Proof. By the tower property, $E[w_{\mathrm{ATO}}(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi,\mathbf Y)]=E[E[Y_i|T_i^\pi=1,X_i]|T_i^\pi=1]=\int E[Y_i|T_i^\pi=1,X_i]dP_{X_i|T_i^\pi=1}$. Since $T_i^\pi$ only depends on $X_i$ by construction, we have the strong ignorability property that $\{Y_i(0),Y_i(1)\}\perp\!\!\!\perp T_i^\pi|X_i$. Therefore, $\int E[Y_i|T_i^\pi=1,X_i]dP_{X_i|T_i^\pi=1}=\int\mu_1(X_i)dP_{X_i|T_i^\pi=1}$. For discrete $X_i$, this is equal to $\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\mu_1(x)P(X_i=x|T_i^\pi=1)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\mu_1(x)\frac{\pi(x)P(X_i=x)}{\sum_{z\in\mathcal X}\pi(z)P(X_i=z)}$. The $\pi$ function that maximizes this is exactly that given in Proposition 6.'

PDF p. 16: 'Proposition 7 (ATT Best Response). Suppose $\Pi$ is the set of all functions $\pi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, and suppose $X$ is a discrete random variable supported on $\mathcal X$. Then the agent's best response to $w_{\mathrm{ATT}}$ is: $\pi^{w_{\mathrm{ATT}}}(x)=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }x\in\arg\max_x\tau(x)\text{ and }\tau(x)>0\\0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$ Proof. $E[w_{\mathrm{ATT}}(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi,\mathbf Y)]=E[Y_i-\hat\mu_0(X_i)|T_i^\pi=1]=E[Y_i|T_i^\pi=1]-E[E[\hat\mu_0(X_i)|T_i^\pi=1,X_i]|T_i^\pi=1]$. Since $E[\hat\mu_0(x)]=\mu_0(x)$ for all $x\in\mathcal X$, we have $E[\hat\mu_0(X_i)|T_i^\pi=1,X_i]=\mu_0(X_i)$. Thus, $E[w_{\mathrm{ATT}}(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi,\mathbf Y)]=E[Y_i|T_i^\pi=1]-E[\mu_0(X_i)|T_i^\pi=1]$. Since we have ignorability in $X_i$, $E[Y_i|T_i^\pi=1]=E[E[Y_i|T_i^\pi=1,X_i]|T_i^\pi=1]=E[E[Y_i(1)|X_i]|T_i^\pi=1]=E[\mu_1(X_i)|T_i^\pi=1]$. Combining these, $E[w_{\mathrm{ATT}}(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi,\mathbf Y)]=E[\mu_1(X_i)-\mu_0(X_i)|T_i^\pi=1]=E[\tau(X_i)|T_i^\pi=1]$. For discrete $X_i$, this is equal to $\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\tau(x)P(X_i=x|T_i^\pi=1)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}\tau(x)\frac{\pi(x)P(X_i=x)}{\sum_{z\in\mathcal X}\pi(z)P(X_i=z)}$. The $\pi$ function that maximizes this is exactly that given in Proposition 7.'

Section 3 states the same rules. PDF p. 4: 'The agent's unconstrained best response is $\pi^{w_{\mathrm{ATO}}}(x)=\mathbb 1(x\in\arg\max_x\mu_1(x)\text{ and }\mu_1(x)>0)$.' and (p. 4) 'the measure of an average outcome instead of a total outcome means that the agent will only treat the single patient with the covariate value $x$ that maximizes $\mu_1$.' PDF p. 5: 'The agent's unconstrained best response is $\pi^{w_{\mathrm{ATT}}}(x)=\mathbb 1(x\in\arg\max_x\tau(x)\text{ and }\tau(x)>0)$. The resulting regret is bounded, but still not zero.' and 'This means that in the best response, the agent only treats patients with the single value $x$ with maximum treatment effect $\tau(x)$.'
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $w_{\mathrm{ATO}}$, $w_{\mathrm{ATT}}$: Reward Functions 1 and 2, PDF p. 4, quoted in (S4). $\mu_t$, $\tau$, $T_i^\pi$: PDF p. 3, (S1). Best response $\pi^w=\arg\max_{\pi\in\Pi}E[w(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi,\mathbf Y)]$: PDF pp. 3 and 14, (S2). Assumption 1: PDF p. 4, (S5). The expectation $E[w(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi,\mathbf Y)]$ is over the $n$ i.i.d. units and the treatment randomization ((S9)); the rewards equal $0$ when no unit is treated.
canonical_claim.note: The statements as printed for finding P006-E001 (Major). Both are refuted by target P006-T1 (as best responses to the rewards as defined, for finite $n$); the corrected statement is target P006-T2. The first equality of each proof equates the unconditional expected reward with the conditional mean among treated units, which omits the probability that somebody is treated. Proposition 7 bears on headline claim P006-H2 as well, and its proof also contains the inference from Assumption 1 that finding P006-E002 concerns.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Assumption 1 with the inference drawn from it in the proof of Proposition 9; Proposition 9 (TT Best Response) and Proposition 3 (TT Regret), as printed
canonical_claim.location: PDF p. 4 (Assumption 1); PDF p. 5 (Reward Function 3, Proposition 3); PDF p. 17 (Proposition 9 and proof); PDF p. 18 (Proposition 3 and proof)
canonical_claim.statement:
PDF p. 4: 'Assumption 1. The principal accesses an estimator $\hat\mu_0(x)$ which is unbiased: $E[\hat\mu_0(x)]=\mu_0(x)\ \forall x\in\mathcal X$.'

PDF p. 5: 'Reward Function 3 (TT): $w_{\mathrm{TT}}(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi,\mathbf Y)=\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-\hat\mu_0(X_i))T_i^\pi$. The agent's unconstrained best response is $\pi^{w_{\mathrm{TT}}}(x)=\mathbb 1(\tau(x)>0)$, which yields zero regret. Proposition 3 (TT Regret). If $\hat\mu_0(x)$ is unbiased, then the regret is $R(\pi^{w_{\mathrm{TT}}})=0$. The regret is zero regardless of the feasible set $\Pi$.'

PDF p. 17: 'Proposition 9 (TT Best Response). Suppose $\Pi$ is the set of all functions $\pi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$. Then the agent's best response to $w_{\mathrm{TT}}$ is: $\pi^{w_{\mathrm{TT}}}(x)=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }\tau(x)>0\\0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$ Proof. $E[w_{\mathrm{TT}}(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi,\mathbf Y)]=nE[Y_i-\hat\mu_0(X_i)|T_i^\pi=1]P(T_i^\pi=1)$. Since we have ignorability in $X_i$, we have $E[Y_i|T_i^\pi=1]=E[\mu_1(X_i)|T_i^\pi=1]$. (shown in more detail in the above proofs). Since $E[\hat\mu_0(x)]=\mu_0(x)$ for all $x\in\mathcal X$, we have $E[\hat\mu_0(X_i)|T_i^\pi=1]=E[\mu_0(X_i)|T_i^\pi=1]$. Thus, $E[w_{\mathrm{TT}}(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi,\mathbf Y)]=nE[\tau(X_i)|T_i^\pi=1]P(T_i^\pi=1)=nV(\pi)$. Applying Lemma 1, the $\pi$ function that maximizes this is exactly that given in Proposition 9.'

PDF p. 18: 'Proposition 3 (TT Regret). If $E[\hat\mu_0(X)]=\mu_0(X)$, then the regret from applying the reward function $w_{TT}$ is $R(\pi^{w_{TT}})=0$. Proof. As shown in Proposition 9, $E[w_{\mathrm{TT}}(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi,\mathbf Y)]=nE[\tau(X_i)|T_i^\pi=1]P(T_i^\pi=1)=nV(\pi)$. Therefore, the agent's best response $\pi^{w_{\mathrm{TT}}}$ also maximizes $V(\pi)$ over the same feasible set, $\Pi$.'
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $V$, $R$, $\pi^w$: PDF p. 3, quoted in (S2)-(S3). $\mu_t$, $\tau$: PDF p. 3, (S1). Lemma 1 and $V(\pi)=E[\tau(X_i)|T_i^\pi=1]P(T_i^\pi=1)$: PDF pp. 15-16, quoted in (S6). The estimator $\hat\mu_0$ may be random; Assumption 1 as printed constrains only $E[\hat\mu_0(x)]$ at each fixed $x$.
canonical_claim.note: The statements as printed for finding P006-E002 (Moderate), chosen because Proposition 3 is the central alignment result (headline claim P006-H3). With Assumption 1 as the only condition on the estimator they are refuted by witness A of target P006-T4 (regret $\frac12$); the corrected statement is target P006-T6. They hold as printed for an estimator independent of the evaluation sample. The same inference appears in the proofs of Proposition 7 (PDF p. 16), Theorem 1 (PDF p. 19) and Theorem 3 (PDF p. 22), whose printed statements are transcribed in targets P006-T26, P006-T7 and P006-T8.

canonical_claim.location: PDF p. 4 (Section 3); PDF p. 17 (Appendix B.4, restatement and proof)
canonical_claim.statement:
PDF p. 4: 'Proposition 1 (ATO Regret). If the conditional mean untreated potential outcomes $\mu_0(x)$ are unbounded, then the regret for the reward function $w_{\mathrm{ATO}}$ may be arbitrarily large.' (Restated in the same words on PDF p. 17.)

The construction that proves it (PDF p. 17): 'We construct an family of distributions for which the regret is unbounded. Let $\mathcal X=\{0,1\}$ with $P(X_i=1)=p$, and let $\mu_1(0)=0$, $\mu_1(1)=1$. Let $\mu_0(0)=\alpha$, and $\mu_0(1)=\beta$. Suppose $\Pi$ is the set of all functions $\pi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$. For $w_{\mathrm{ATO}}$, the agent's best response is $\pi^{w_{\mathrm{ATO}}}(0)=0$ and $\pi^{w_{\mathrm{ATO}}}(1)=1$. We illustrate two failure modes for the reward function $w_{\mathrm{ATO}}$. First, suppose $\alpha<0$, and $\beta=0$. Then the regret is given by $R(\pi^w)=\max_{\pi\in\Pi}V(\pi)-V(\pi^w)=-\alpha(1-p)+p-p=-\alpha(1-p)$. This is unbounded for unbounded $\alpha$.'

Formal reading (the paper's 'may be arbitrarily large'): for every $M>0$ there are a distribution of $(X_i,Y_i(0),Y_i(1))$ and a best response $\pi^{w_{\mathrm{ATO}}}\in\arg\max_{\pi\in\Pi}E[w_{\mathrm{ATO}}(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi,\mathbf Y)]$, with $\Pi$ the set of all functions $\pi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, such that $R(\pi^{w_{\mathrm{ATO}}})>M$. In the family above, with $p\in(0,1)$, potential outcomes with the stated conditional means, and $\pi=(a,b)$, $a=\pi(0)$, $b=\pi(1)$:
(i) for every $n\geq2$ the unique best response to $w_{\mathrm{ATO}}$ is $(a,b)=(0,1)$ (for $n=1$ the best responses are the policies with $b=1$ and $a$ arbitrary);
(ii) in the first failure mode ($\alpha<0$, $\beta=0$): $\tau(0)=-\alpha>0$, $\tau(1)=1$, $\max_{\pi\in\Pi}V(\pi)=-\alpha(1-p)+p$, $V(0,1)=p$ and $R(\pi^w)=-\alpha(1-p)$, which tends to $\infty$ as $\alpha\to-\infty$ with $p$ fixed.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $w_{\mathrm{ATO}}$: Reward Function 1, PDF p. 4, quoted in (S4). $\mu_t$, $\tau$: PDF p. 3, (S1). $V$, $R$, $\pi^w$: PDF p. 3, (S2)-(S3); $V(\pi)=E[\pi(X_i)\tau(X_i)]$ by the proof of Lemma 1 ((S6)). The exact expected reward of $w_{\mathrm{ATO}}$ for finite $n$: target P006-T2, here with $A=pb$ and $q=pb+(1-p)a$, so that $E[w_{\mathrm{ATO}}]=h_n(q)\,pb$ with $h_n$ strictly decreasing on $[0,1]$ for $n\geq2$.
canonical_claim.note: Headline result (the first sentence of headline claim P006-H1). The statement held up for both readers. Two findings touch its proof and not its conclusion: the proof takes its best response from the rule of Proposition 6, which is not valid in general (finding P006-E001), so (i) is to be proved from the exact finite-$n$ reward (the validator's derivation of P006-E001, section 7, does this); and the display for the second failure mode has a sign error (finding P006-E007, targets P006-T18 and P006-T19). The first failure mode alone proves the proposition.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proposition 4 ($w_{\mathrm{TT}}$ used directly as a score violates both ranking properties)
canonical_claim.location: PDF p. 6 (Section 4); PDF pp. 18-19 (Appendix C.2, restatement and proof)
canonical_claim.statement:
PDF p. 6: 'Proposition 4. If $w_k$ is directly given by $w_{\mathrm{TT}}$ for each agent $k$, then both ranking properties in Definitions 1 and 2 will be violated.' PDF p. 18: 'Proposition 4. If $w_k(\mathbf X^{(k)},\mathbf T^{\pi_k},\mathbf Y^{(k)})=\sum_{i=1}^{n_k}(Y_i^{(k)}-\hat\mu_0(X_i^{(k)}))T_i^{\pi_k}$, then both ranking properties in Definitions 1 and 2 will be violated.'

The construction that proves it (PDF p. 19): 'Suppose for agents $j$ and $k$, $\Pi_j$ and $\Pi_k$ are both unconstrained. For $w_k$ as defined above, $\max_{\pi_j\in\Pi_j}E[w_j(\mathbf X^{(j)},\mathbf T^{\pi_j},\mathbf Y^{(k)})]=n_jE[\tau^{(j)}(X^{(j)})\mathbb 1(\tau^{(j)}(X^{(j)})>0)]$, $\max_{\pi_k\in\Pi_k}E[w_k(\mathbf X^{(k)},\mathbf T^{\pi_k},\mathbf Y^{(k)})]=n_kE[\tau^{(k)}(X^{(k)})\mathbb 1(\tau^{(k)}(X^{(k)})>0)]$. For Definition 1, suppose $\tau^{(j)}(x)\geq\tau^{(k)}(x)$ for all $x\in\mathcal X$, and $X^{(j)}$ and $X^{(k)}$ are identically distributed. Then, $E[\tau^{(j)}(X^{(j)})\mathbb 1(\tau^{(j)}(X^{(j)})>0)]\geq E[\tau^{(k)}(X^{(k)})\mathbb 1(\tau^{(k)}(X^{(k)})>0)]$. Let $n_j,n_k$ be a pair such that $n_j<n_k\frac{E[\tau^{(k)}(X^{(k)})\mathbb 1(\tau^{(k)}(X^{(k)})>0)]}{E[\tau^{(j)}(X^{(j)})\mathbb 1(\tau^{(j)}(X^{(j)})>0)]}$. This immediately results in Definition 1 being violated. Definition 2 is also violated, since $\tau^{(j)}(x)\geq\tau^{(k)}(x)$ for all $x\in\mathcal X$ implies that $E[\tau^{(j)}(X_0)]\geq E[\tau^{(k)}(X_0)]$ for any reference population $P_{X_0}$. However, for the above $n_j,n_k$, we've shown that $\max_{\pi_j\in\Pi_j}E[w_j(\mathbf X^{(j)},\mathbf T^{\pi_j},\mathbf Y^{(k)})]<\max_{\pi_k\in\Pi_k}E[w_k(\mathbf X^{(k)},\mathbf T^{\pi_k},\mathbf Y^{(k)})]$.'

Formal reading ('will be violated' is an existence statement): there are agents $j,k$ satisfying the multi-agent standing assumptions, with unconstrained feasible sets and scores $w_j=w_k=w_{\mathrm{TT}}$, such that $\tau^{(j)}(x)\geq\tau^{(k)}(x)$ for all $x$ and $E[\tau^{(j)}(X_0)]\geq E[\tau^{(k)}(X_0)]$, and yet $\max_{\pi_j\in\Pi_j}E[w_j(\mathbf X^{(j)},\mathbf T^{\pi_j},\mathbf Y^{(j)})]<\max_{\pi_k\in\Pi_k}E[w_k(\mathbf X^{(k)},\mathbf T^{\pi_k},\mathbf Y^{(k)})]$. The identities used: for each agent, $\max_{\pi_k\in\Pi_k}E[w_k(\mathbf X^{(k)},\mathbf T^{\pi_k},\mathbf Y^{(k)})]=n_kE[\tau^{(k)}(X^{(k)})\mathbb 1(\tau^{(k)}(X^{(k)})>0)]$; and whenever $X^{(j)}$ and $X^{(k)}$ are identically distributed, $\tau^{(j)}\geq\tau^{(k)}$ pointwise, $E[\tau^{(k)}(X^{(k)})\mathbb 1(\tau^{(k)}(X^{(k)})>0)]>0$ and $n_jE[\tau^{(j)}(X^{(j)})\mathbb 1(\tau^{(j)}(X^{(j)})>0)]<n_kE[\tau^{(k)}(X^{(k)})\mathbb 1(\tau^{(k)}(X^{(k)})>0)]$, both definitions fail for the pair $(j,k)$. For instance $\tau^{(j)}=\tau^{(k)}\equiv1$, $n_j=1$, $n_k=2$ gives best scores $1<2$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Definitions 1 and 2: PDF p. 5 (transcribed, and corrected to each agent's own sample, in target P006-T14). Several agents, $n_k$, $P_{X^k}$, $\mu^k_0=\mu_0$, $\tau^{(k)}$, $w_k$: PDF p. 5 and Appendix C.1, PDF p. 18, quoted in (S7). $w_{\mathrm{TT}}$: Reward Function 3, PDF p. 5, (S4). The identity for the best score rests on $E[w_{\mathrm{TT}}]=n_kV(\pi_k)$ (Proposition 9, PDF p. 17), which needs the condition on the estimator of target P006-T6 (true for a nonrandom $\hat\mu_0=\mu_0$).
canonical_claim.note: Headline result (the first part of headline claim P006-H4). It held up for both readers, who read 'will be violated' as 'can be violated' for a suitable pair of agents. The printed displays write $\mathbf Y^{(k)}$ in agent $j$'s score (finding P006-E013, target P006-T14); the formal reading uses $\mathbf Y^{(j)}$. The pair $n_j,n_k$ of the proof exists only if both positive-part expectations are positive, which the formal reading states. The estimator enters through Proposition 9 (finding P006-E002).
